column1: # clues.tsv for ft_convert_base — pedagogic hints only. NEVER state the expected value or the fix.
# Format: <hint><TAB><member CASE label><TAB>...   (fires if ANY member case fails)
# Lines are shown most-fundamental first; the first line doubles as the "foothold".

Before you touch the number, both bases have to earn the right to be used. C 04 lists invalid bases twice, once for writing a number in a base (ft_putnbr_base) and once for reading one (ft_atoi_base), and C 07 says which of the two nbr follows. Which list governs base_from, which governs base_to, and what do you hand back when either base fails its list?

What is nbr before it is written in base_to: which quantity does the string stand for? Have you met both halves of this job before, turning a string written in a base into a number and a number into a string in a base? What did each of them have to handle, and are you keeping their rules apart?

Which arithmetic peels one digit off a quantity in a given base, and at which end of the result does that digit belong? What does a symbol's position in base_to stand for: so does case matter, and can the symbols be anything the caller chose? Where does a negative value's sign go?
nbr follows ft_atoi_base's rules, which are ft_atoi's: whitespace, signs and digits each have their place in the string. What does that order make of a whitespace byte that comes after a sign?
What does repeated division produce when the quantity is already nothing? Make sure that path still emits one symbol — which one, and where does base_to say to find it?

The most negative value cannot be flipped to its positive twin inside the same signed width. Can you read its symbols without ever holding that impossible positive in a type too small for it on some platform? (What C promises about the width of each type: docs/testing.md, under ilp32.)
